name: SimPLe (Simulated Policy Learning)
analogy: Think of it as a flight simulator for a trading rookie. First you record a modest amount of real market behaviour and build a simulator from it. Then the rookie practises thousands of sessions in the simulator, and only occasionally steps into the real market to check that the simulator still feels right.

steps.title: Gather a small amount of real experience
steps.description: The agent first acts in the real environment for a short while, using a rough policy, and records what it saw, what it did and what reward followed. Real data is treated as scarce and valuable.
steps.inExample: A starter rule trades through 20,000 real five-minute MNQ bars from the training window, and every bar, action and reward is recorded.

steps.title: Teach a world model to predict the next bars
steps.description: A sequence model is trained to predict what the next bars will look like after each action. It outputs a full picture of the next observation, not a compressed code, and it includes a random element so it can produce more than one plausible future.
steps.inExample: Given the last 20 bars and an action to go long, the world model produces the next bar's open, high, low, close and volume, with some randomness each time.

steps.title: Make the world model behave like a real environment
steps.description: The world model is wrapped so that it answers the same calls a real market environment would: reset to a starting point and step forward one bar. Imagined episodes are kept short, because small errors compound the further the simulator runs from a real starting bar.
steps.inExample: The simulator starts an episode from a random real window and then steps 30 bars (150 minutes of five-minute bars), handing back imagined bars and rewards.

steps.title: Train an ordinary policy entirely inside the simulator
steps.description: A standard learning method for choosing actions is run for a long time against the simulator. Because simulated bars cost nothing, it can practise far more than the real record would allow.
steps.inExample: The policy trains on 2,000 simulated 30-bar episodes, learning to be long when the imagined bars drift up and flat when they chop sideways.

steps.title: Return to the real market to correct the model
steps.description: The improved policy is run in the real environment for a short stretch. That fresh real data shows where the simulator was wrong, particularly in situations the policy now visits that the first data never covered.
steps.inExample: The new policy trades another 5,000 real bars, and the model is found to have underestimated how often prices gap at the open.

steps.title: Repeat the loop of real data, model, and practice
steps.description: The world model is retrained with the extra real data and the policy is practised again. Each cycle makes the simulator more faithful where the policy actually goes.
steps.inExample: After 4 cycles the policy's simulated and real results are close enough that the loop stops.

useFor.task: Learning a trading policy from limited history
useFor.example: Training a position policy for a thinly traded futures contract where only a few months of five-minute bars exist.

useFor.task: Trying many policy designs against one fixed simulator
useFor.example: Comparing five different reward settings for an MNQ policy without paying for new real-market runs each time.
Each weekend adding the week's new bars to the world model and retraining the policy on the refreshed simulator.

useFor.task: Stress-testing a policy on imagined paths
useFor.example: Running a finished policy through thousands of simulated episodes to see how it behaves in sequences the historical record only shows once or twice.

avoidWhen: The simulator is clearly inaccurate, for example after a regime change; a policy trained inside a wrong world learns to exploit its flaws, and a method that checks the real market on every decision is safer.
A simple supervised model on engineered features already answers the question; building a world model and a policy is much heavier than predicting direction.

example.scenario: A research run on MNQ five-minute bars has finished its second cycle. The policy was trained inside the learned simulator and is now asked what to hold at the 11:00 bar.

input.summary: The recent bars and current position, which the trained policy reads exactly as it did inside the simulator.

fields.name: close
fields.meaning: The price at which the 11:00 five-minute bar closed.

fields.name: recent bars read
fields.meaning: The window of history the policy sees as its state.

fields.name: average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: The typical high-to-low travel of a recent bar.

fields.name: current position
fields.meaning: No contracts held going into the decision.

fields.name: real bars used to build the simulator
fields.meaning: How much real history the world model has learned from so far.

fields.name: simulated episodes practised
fields.meaning: How many imagined stretches of trading the policy trained on.

output.summary: The policy's chance of choosing each action, and the action it takes.

fields.name: chance of going short
fields.meaning: How strongly the policy favours a short position on this bar.

fields.name: chance of staying flat
fields.meaning: How strongly the policy favours doing nothing.

fields.name: chance of going long
fields.meaning: How strongly the policy favours a long position.

fields.name: action taken
fields.meaning: The option chosen from those chances.

example.reading: The policy leans long but is far from sure, since flat is almost as likely. Compare its simulated results with its results on real held-out bars: a large gap means the simulator is flattering the policy and the real market result is the one to trust.
